content: Avian influenza, commonly referred to as bird flu, is an illness caused by a virus that primarily infects wild and domestic birds. Wild birds that are known to carry bird flu viruses include migratory waterbirds such as ducks, geese, and swans, as well as shorebirds like storks. These viruses can easily spread from wild birds to domestic poultry, including chickens, turkeys, geese, and pheasants. The virus is present in the feces (droppings) of infected birds, as well as in fluids from their eyes, noses, or mouths. Although bird flu viruses do not typically infect humans, transmission can occur under certain circumstances. This may happen if you touch your eyes, nose, or mouth after handling infected live or dead birds, or after coming into contact with surfaces or objects contaminated with bird flu viruses. Additionally, inhaling droplets or dust contaminated with the virus can lead to infection. Individuals infected with bird flu may experience a range of symptoms, from no symptoms at all to severe illness. Mild symptoms can include eye redness (conjunctivitis), cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headaches, and fatigue. More severe symptoms may involve high fever, shortness of breath, and difficulty breathing. In cases of severe disease, pneumonia may develop, potentially requiring hospitalization. Less common symptoms include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Most travelers are at low risk of contracting bird flu. However, individuals who work closely with animals, such as veterinarians, farmers, animal industry professionals, and wildlife specialists, or those who visit poultry farms or live-animal markets, may face a higher risk of exposure. To reduce the risk of bird flu infection, travelers should take the following precautions: Avoid touching birds and refrain from visiting areas where birds are kept, such as poultry farms, live-animal markets, or other locations where live poultry are raised, housed, slaughtered, or sold. If visiting such places is unavoidable, wear a well-fitting face mask and avoid direct contact with poultry or other birds. When visiting wetlands or outdoor areas where birds live, take measures to minimize exposure to germs during and after your visit. Do not touch sick or dead wild birds or poultry. Wash your hands frequently with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after contact with birds, bird habitats, or uncooked poultry. If soap and water are unavailable, use a hand sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol to clean your hands. Avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth. If you must touch your face, ensure your hands are clean beforehand. Avoid close contact, such as kissing, hugging, or sharing eating utensils or cups, with individuals who are sick. By following these preventive measures, travelers can significantly reduce their risk of exposure to bird flu.
